clue.text: Puts on a good front before make-up?

parts.note: pre- is the Latin-derived prefix meaning before
putting on one's face is applying make-up, so faces stands for make-up here

explanation.surface: Someone putting on a brave show before an argument is patched up.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads as keeping up appearances, but a writer who prefaces a book literally puts something at its front.
explanation.definitionFit: To preface a text is to set an introduction at its start, a front placed before the rest.

clue.text: Try the piano if the cast is so silly

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
to cast is to fling or throw

explanation.surface: Someone told to give the piano a go if the plaster cast makes other things silly.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivial, worthless talk is twaddle, and the adjective means trivial and silly.

clue.text: Old men of the Five Towns.?

definitions.text: Old men of the Five Towns

parts.words: Old men of the Five Towns
parts.note: Etruria is a district of Stoke in the Five Towns, and also the ancient land of an early Italian people

explanation.surface: A question about the elderly residents of the Potteries.
explanation.walkthrough: The Five Towns are Arnold Bennett's name for the Potteries around Stoke-on-Trent, England, where Wedgwood named his works Etruria after the ancient Italian region.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient people of Etruria in Italy were old men in that sense, and Etruria is also a district of the Potteries.

parts.note: a jenny is a female donkey and neddy a pet name for a male one

explanation.surface: Two people with homely British names.
explanation.walkthrough: Both look like people's names; a jenny is a female donkey and 'neddy' is British slang for a donkey.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of donkeys, a female and a male, are together plural donkeys.

clue.text: It's lace throughout, just the thing for spring

indicators.note: throughout is read as through and out, the letters worked over into a new order

explanation.surface: A dressmaker praising an all-lace garment for the warmer season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spring' suggests the season, but it means springiness or stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretchy material that returns to shape gives springiness, so it is just what a spring needs.

indicators.note: before tells us the word as stands in front of the word for forwarded

parts.note: a letter forwarded is one sent on

explanation.surface: A clerk confirming a document was passed on exactly as it went last time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' looks like part of the phrase 'as before', meaning 'as previously', but it is the order signal for the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying yes gives agreement, and agreement or consent is what this noun names.

clue.text: Thrifty type almost naked in the forest

parts.note: a thrifty person is a saver

indicators.note: almost means the word naked loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A frugal person running about nearly nude among the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: SAVERNAKE Forest is an ancient woodland in Wiltshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Savernake is the name of a large ancient English woodland, so it is a forest by name.

parts.note: read as a description of the whole state of weariness, not a painting

explanation.surface: Someone looking utterly fed up.
explanation.definitionFit: This borrowed French word names listless weariness, the very image of being bored.

parts.note: the ... Girls were a famous dance troupe, and the steering bar of a boat guides it at sea

explanation.surface: A member of the youth organisation sailing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Girl Guide' reads as the youth movement, but it splits: a Tiller Girl was a high-kicking British dancer, and this bar guides a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: The lever that turns a boat's rudder steers or guides it at sea.

clue.text: So the clodhopper goes for his potatoes

definitions.text: So the clodhopper goes for his potatoes

parts.words: So the clodhopper goes for his potatoes
parts.note: a clodhopper walks heavily, and farmers store potatoes in earth-covered heaps of the same name

explanation.surface: A heavy-footed farm worker trudging off to fetch potatoes.
explanation.walkthrough: A clodhopper treads heavily (clamps along); a clamp is also a mound of potatoes stored under straw and earth on a farm.
explanation.definitionFit: To tread heavily is to clump, and stored heaps of root crops covered with earth go by the same name.

clue.text: Stop one getting a front seat?

parts.note: fore means the front part, as in the fore of a ship
a stall is a seat, as in the stalls of a theatre or a choir stall

explanation.surface: Someone queuing early to stop a rival grabbing the front-row seat at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: In British theatres the stalls are the seats on the ground floor nearest the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: To head off an action by acting first is to stop or prevent it.

definitions.meaning: a rare sense from Latin vena, vein: relating to the veins, hence to blood

explanation.surface: An angry exclamation that someone is utterly crooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' reads as a British swear word intensifying 'corrupt', but it is a separate definition: the rare sense 'of the veins'.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the rare 'of the veins' (blood vessels); the usual sense describes an official willing to take bribes.

parts.note: the competitors' names are written on rolls, and the jousting ground itself bears the same name

explanation.surface: A notice about who has signed up for the competitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Rolls of names record entries, and in medieval usage the enclosed ground for jousting was also called by this word.

parts.note: refers to J. M. W. Turner's famous painting of a warship towed to be broken up

explanation.surface: A reference to a celebrated painting of a warship.
explanation.walkthrough: J. M. W. Turner was an English painter; 'The Fighting Temeraire' (1839) shows the old warship towed to the breaker's yard.
explanation.definitionFit: HMS Temeraire, the ship that fought at Trafalgar, is the vessel shown in Turner's famous painting.

clue.text: Not one hit of elegance, might have come out of the ark!

definitions.text: might have come out of the ark

parts.note: no is a word for not, as in no better
a is the indefinite article, meaning one
chic means stylish elegance, here a dose or hit of it

explanation.surface: A scornful remark that something so old-fashioned has no style at all and dates from the Flood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of the ark' is an idiom for very old-fashioned; the answer is the adjective from Noah, whose ark it was.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means relating to Noah, so anything from his ark fits it.

parts.note: split as a goat found on high ground: a male goat is a billy, and the high ground is a hill

explanation.surface: A nimble climbing animal.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a hill billy, a goat on a hill; the word itself means a backwoods mountain dweller.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustic from remote mountain country is called this, and literally it is a billy goat on high ground.

parts.note: bosky means wooded and shady, and spirits are ghosts; one word means both shady places and ghosts

explanation.surface: Woodland ghosts haunting a shady copse.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both ghosts and the shadowy spots under trees that bosky woodland gives.

clue.text: Put in a case but not for show

definitions.text: Put in a case but not for show

parts.words: Put in a case but not for show
parts.note: covering something in a scabbard or sleeve to protect it, not placing it in a display case

explanation.surface: Advice on packing away a precious object rather than exhibiting it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' suggests a glass display case; the sense is a sword's scabbard or sheath.
explanation.definitionFit: To enclose a blade in a scabbard is to put it in a protective case.

clue.text: Uncle makes his with a feeling of security

definitions.text: Uncle makes his with a feeling of security

parts.words: Uncle makes his with a feeling of security
parts.note: uncle is slang for a pawnbroker, who lends money safe in holding pledged goods

explanation.surface: A relative making romantic moves while feeling safe.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang the pawnbroker is called 'uncle'; he lends money against goods, so he has security.
explanation.definitionFit: Loans of money are this word, as are amorous overtures an uncle might make.

parts.note: an inn's stable worker who looked after travellers' horses was the old equivalent of a garage attendant

explanation.surface: A question about who did the garage worker's job in his own era.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'the garage-hand's counterpart in his day': where travellers now have cars serviced, they once had horses stabled at an inn.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn's stableman tending horses did for coaching travellers what a garage hand does for motorists.

parts.note: the famous line from the last chapter of Jane Eyre, addressed to the person holding the book

explanation.surface: A quotation from a famous novel with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre opens its final chapter with the narrator speaking directly to the one turning its pages.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Eyre addresses the person perusing the novel, so the missing word names that perusing person.

parts.note: the word for holy is also used ironically as a mild curse, as in 'the whole wretched thing'

explanation.surface: A remark on how a word can mean its own opposite when used politely.
explanation.definitionFit: Holy or sanctified in its usual sense, it is also a polite stand-in for damned, as in 'not a single one'.

clue.text: Ferdinand and I get on being massively rich

parts.note: Ferdinand the Bull is the hero of a famous children's story
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Ferdinand and the speaker prospering together hugely.
explanation.walkthrough: Ferdinand is a name, but here it is the gentle bull of Munro Leaf's children's book 'The Story of Ferdinand'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold or silver in bars is solid wealth in bulk, the stuff of the hugely rich.

definitions.meaning: to be sparing with, as in skimping on supplies
periods of assigned duty, as in a spell of work

explanation.surface: A manager reducing the jobs given to staff.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp on something is one sense; a spell of assigned work, a shift, is the other.

parts.note: handy hints at the hand; a brief sketch takes this name, and the pad is the hard plate on the tip of a digit

explanation.surface: An advertisement for a small, convenient drawing pad.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief outline is called by this name, and the horny plate on the end of the shortest digit is literally one.

clue.text: There's colour showing in the cucumber frame

indicators.note: showing in says the colour's letters can be seen inside these words

explanation.surface: A gardener noting something coloured inside the glass frame where cucumbers grow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frame' suggests a garden cold frame, but the run is inside 'cucumber'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an earthy brown pigment, a natural colour used in paints.

clue.text: What the Italian defines as a portion of lobster

parts.note: che is Italian for what
la is the Italian feminine word for the

explanation.surface: An Italian speaker explaining what a piece of lobster is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian' governs both words: CHE is Italian 'what' and LA Italian 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: This zoological term names the pincer or claw of a crustacean, a part of a lobster.

parts.note: Thalia is the Greek Muse of comedy, so her art is the funny kind

explanation.surface: Someone praising a witty friend named Thalia.
explanation.walkthrough: Thalia looks like a friend's name; in Greek myth she is the Muse of comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Muse of comedy presides over what is funny, and the word means both funny and a comedian.

clue.text: Prizeman might turn tail to become a peer

indicators.note: turn tail tells us the last letters of the word for peer swap round

parts.note: a peer of the realm is a noble

explanation.surface: A prizewinner who might run away to join the aristocracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn tail' usually means flee; here it swaps the last two letters, so NOBLE becomes NOBEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Nobel founded the famous prizes, so a prizewinner bears his name as laureate.

parts.note: points to Elgar's Enigma Variations, whose hidden theme still puzzles listeners

explanation.surface: A remark that musical variations can be hard to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: Elgar's 'Enigma Variations' is an English orchestral work with a famously unexplained hidden theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Elgar's Variations carry the title Enigma, and something enigmatic is mysterious and baffling.

clue.text: Saint fishes for lost. sheep perhaps

parts.note: rays are flat fishes such as skates

explanation.surface: A holy figure out fishing, in the manner of the gospels, for those gone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the apostles as fishers of men; 'for' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that have wandered off are called this, lost sheep being an example.

parts.note: a horse laugh is a coarse guffaw, but here read literally as the soft neighing noises a horse makes

explanation.surface: Loud coarse guffaws.
explanation.definitionFit: Muffled sniggers are called this, and a horse's soft whinny is a nicker or snicker.
